main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of principles of Food and Nutrition
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the dietary needs for different groups of people
learning_activity_name: Explain the concept of groups with special dietary needs (meaning, category and reasons)
sla_name: Groups with special dietary needs
sla_assessment_criteria: The concept of groups with special dietary needs is well explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts depicting categories of groups with special dietary needs
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Certain groups of people have nutritional requirements that differ from the general population because of age, physiological state, health condition or lifestyle choice.
sla_notes_details: A group with special dietary needs is any category of people whose nutrient requirements, food restrictions or feeding practices differ from the average healthy adult due to factors such as growth, pregnancy, illness or personal choice. Categories include children and adolescents (needing extra nutrients for growth), pregnant and lactating women (needing extra energy, protein, iron and folic acid), elders (often needing fewer calories but the same or higher micronutrient intake), vegetarians (excluding animal-based foods and needing planned protein and vitamin B12 sources), and invalids and convalescents (people recovering from illness who need easily digestible, nutrient-dense foods). Reasons for these differences include the body's changing physiological demands, digestive capacity and any medical conditions present.
sla_notes_illustrations: A pregnant woman is classified in a special dietary needs group because her body requires extra iron and folic acid to support the developing baby, unlike a non-pregnant woman of the same age.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding these groups helps a family or community health worker in Tanzania plan appropriate meals for a breastfeeding mother, an elderly grandparent and a growing child within the same household.
sla_exercise: Define a group with special dietary needs.::A category of people whose nutrient requirements or feeding practices differ from the average healthy adult due to factors such as growth, pregnancy, illness or choice.||Name three groups with special dietary needs.::Children/adolescents, pregnant and lactating women, and elders (or vegetarians, invalids and convalescents).||Why do pregnant women need more iron and folic acid than other adults?::To support the increased blood volume and the growth and development of the baby.

learning_activity_name: Analyse the nutritional requirements for each special group (children, adolescents, elders, vegetarians, pregnant women and lactating mothers, invalids and convalescents)
sla_name: Nutritional requirements for special groups
sla_assessment_criteria: Nutritional requirements for each group are well analysed.
sla_teaching_aids: Charts depicting nutritional requirements for different special groups of people. Food composition tables
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Each special group has specific nutrient requirements that must be analysed individually to plan appropriate diets.
sla_notes_details: Children and adolescents require higher amounts of protein, calcium and energy relative to body weight to support rapid growth and bone development. Elders generally need reduced energy intake due to lower activity levels but continued or increased intake of calcium, vitamin D and fibre to protect bone health and digestion. Vegetarians need carefully planned intake of protein (from legumes, nuts and dairy if allowed), iron, zinc and vitamin B12, since these are more concentrated in animal foods. Pregnant women need extra folic acid (to prevent neural tube defects), iron (for increased blood volume) and calcium, while lactating mothers need additional energy and fluids to support milk production. Invalids and convalescents need easily digestible, energy- and protein-dense foods to support recovery and rebuild body tissue.
sla_notes_illustrations: A nutritionist analysing the needs of an adolescent athlete, a pregnant woman and an elderly person in the same community would recommend different quantities of protein, iron and calcium for each, based on their distinct physiological requirements.
sla_notes_daily_life: Health centres and community nutrition programmes in Tanzania routinely analyse these requirements when advising mothers, the elderly and patients recovering from illness on what to eat.
sla_exercise: Why do children and adolescents need more protein and calcium relative to their body weight?::To support rapid growth and bone development.||Name one nutrient that vegetarians must plan carefully to obtain enough of.::Vitamin B12 (or iron, zinc or protein).||What type of food is most suitable for an invalid or convalescent recovering from illness?::Easily digestible, energy- and protein-dense foods that support recovery and rebuild body tissue.

learning_activity_name: Explain the concept of Nutrients values (meaning, types, uses and major factors considered in developing nutrient values)
sla_name: The concept of nutrient values
sla_assessment_criteria: The concept of Nutrients value is well explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Food composition tables|RDA/NRV’s tables
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Nutrient values describe the standardised amounts of specific nutrients that foods provide or that individuals require, and they are essential tools for planning healthy diets.
sla_notes_details: Nutrient values refer to figures showing the type and amount of nutrients (such as protein, energy, vitamins and minerals) contained in foods or required by individuals. Types of nutrient value tables include Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDA), Nutrient Reference Values (NRV), and food composition tables that list nutrient content per 100 grams of a food item. These values are used to plan balanced meals, assess whether an individual's diet meets their needs, and design nutrition intervention programmes. Major factors considered when developing nutrient values include age, sex, body weight, physiological state (such as pregnancy), physical activity level, and the health status of the population being studied.
sla_notes_illustrations: A food composition table showing that 100 grams of maize flour provides a certain amount of energy and protein allows a planner to calculate how much maize flour a family needs to meet their daily energy requirement.
sla_notes_daily_life: Nutrition labels on packaged foods sold in Tanzanian shops display nutrient values so consumers can check how much energy, sugar or fat a product contains before buying it.
sla_exercise: What is meant by nutrient values?::Figures showing the type and amount of nutrients that foods provide or that individuals require.||Name one type of nutrient value table.::Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) table (or Nutrient Reference Value (NRV) table, or food composition table).||State one factor considered when developing nutrient values.::Age (or sex, body weight, physiological state, or activity level).

sla_assessment_criteria: Nutritional requirements of each group are determined.

sla_notes_intro: RDA and NRV tables provide standard reference values that let a nutrition planner determine how much of each nutrient a specific individual needs.
sla_notes_details: To use RDA/NRV tables, one identifies the individual's age group, sex and physiological state (for example, pregnant, lactating, or none of these), then reads across the table to find the recommended daily amount for each nutrient, such as energy, protein, iron, calcium and vitamins, for that specific category. These values are typically given per day and may be expressed in grams, milligrams or micrograms. Comparing an individual's actual nutrient intake, calculated from the foods they eat, against these RDA/NRV figures shows whether their diet is adequate, deficient or excessive in any nutrient.
sla_notes_illustrations: To find the daily iron requirement of a 16-year-old girl, a student would locate the row for adolescent females in the RDA table and read the recommended milligrams of iron per day directly from that row.
sla_notes_daily_life: Community health workers use RDA/NRV tables in exactly this way when advising mothers on how much of each nutrient their children or themselves need daily.
sla_exercise: What information must be identified about a person before consulting an RDA/NRV table?::Their age group, sex and physiological state (for example, pregnant or lactating).||In what units are RDA/NRV values for nutrients typically expressed?::Grams, milligrams or micrograms per day.||How is an RDA/NRV table used to check if a diet is adequate?::By comparing an individual's actual nutrient intake against the recommended values in the table for their category.

learning_activity_name: Compute the nutrients intake for different groups using food composition tables and compare with RDA
sla_name: Computing nutrient intake using food composition tables
sla_assessment_criteria: Nutrients intake for different groups are well computed and compared with RDA.
sla_teaching_aids: Food composition tables|RDA table
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Food composition tables allow the actual amount of nutrients consumed to be calculated from the foods and quantities eaten, so this can be compared with recommended values.
sla_notes_details: To compute nutrient intake, one records all foods and their exact quantities eaten by an individual over a period (such as one day), looks up each food's nutrient content per 100 grams in a food composition table, calculates the nutrient amount provided by the actual quantity eaten using proportion, and sums the nutrient contributions from all foods eaten to get total daily intake. This total is then compared with the individual's RDA to determine whether their diet is meeting, falling short of, or exceeding their nutritional needs for a given nutrient.
sla_notes_illustrations: If a food composition table shows that 100 grams of rice provides 130 kilocalories and a person eats 300 grams of rice, the energy contributed by that rice is calculated as 130 multiplied by 3, giving 390 kilocalories, which is then added to the energy from all other foods eaten that day.
sla_notes_daily_life: Nutritionists and dietitians in hospitals and community health programmes across Tanzania use this same calculation method to assess whether a patient's or community member's diet meets their nutritional needs.
sla_exercise: What is the first step in computing nutrient intake for an individual?::Recording all the foods and their exact quantities eaten over a period such as one day.||How is the nutrient content of an actual food quantity calculated from a food composition table?::By using proportion based on the nutrient value given per 100 grams of that food.||Why is computed nutrient intake compared with RDA values?::To determine whether the individual's diet meets, falls short of, or exceeds their nutritional needs.

learning_activity_name: Plan meals for each group of individual with special dietary needs based on RDA, food composition table and Tanzania food based dietary guidelines
sla_name: Planning meals for groups with special dietary needs
sla_assessment_criteria: Meals for individuals with special dietary needs are well planned.
sla_teaching_aids: Food composition tables|RDA tables
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Meal planning applies knowledge of nutrient requirements and food composition to design practical, balanced meals suited to a specific group.
sla_notes_details: Planning meals for a group with special dietary needs involves determining the group's RDA for key nutrients, selecting locally available foods from food composition tables that together meet those requirements, following the Tanzania food-based dietary guidelines (which recommend proportions of different food groups such as staples, proteins, fruits and vegetables), and arranging meals across the day to spread nutrient and energy intake appropriately. The planner must also consider the group's practical needs, such as easily digestible foods for the elderly or invalids, or extra iron-rich foods for pregnant women, and the affordability and availability of chosen foods.
sla_notes_illustrations: When planning a day's meals for a pregnant woman, a planner would include iron-rich foods such as beans or liver, together with a vitamin C source like oranges to improve iron absorption, all guided by the Tanzania food-based dietary guidelines.
sla_notes_daily_life: Mothers, school feeding programme organisers and hospital dietitians in Tanzania plan meals this way every day to make sure vulnerable groups receive the nutrients they need from locally available foods.
sla_exercise: Name one document or guideline used when planning meals for a population group in Tanzania.::The Tanzania food-based dietary guidelines.||Why should meals for pregnant women include iron-rich foods alongside a source of vitamin C?::Because vitamin C improves the body's absorption of iron from food.||State one practical factor to consider when planning meals for the elderly.::Choosing easily digestible foods (or affordability and availability of the foods chosen).

learning_activity_name: Describe energy balance (meaning and components of energy expenditure)
sla_name: Energy balance and its components
sla_assessment_criteria: Energy balance concept is well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Weighing scale|Stadiometer
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Energy balance describes the relationship between the energy a person consumes through food and the energy they expend through the body's activities.
sla_notes_details: Energy balance is the state where energy intake (from food and drink) equals energy expenditure (energy used by the body); a positive balance (intake greater than expenditure) leads to weight gain, while a negative balance leads to weight loss. Components of energy expenditure include Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR), the energy used to maintain basic body functions such as breathing and circulation at rest, the thermic effect of food, energy used to digest and process food, and physical activity, energy used in movement and exercise, which is the most variable component. Understanding these components allows individuals to manage body weight and health through balancing food intake with activity level.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student calculating their own energy balance might estimate their BMR using a standard formula, add an estimate of energy used in daily activities and exercise, and compare this total expenditure with the energy they consumed that day from food to see whether they are in positive, negative or balanced energy status.
sla_notes_daily_life: People trying to lose or gain weight in everyday life are managing their own energy balance by adjusting food intake and physical activity, exactly as covered in this competence.
sla_exercise: Define energy balance.::The state where the energy consumed through food equals the energy expended by the body.||Name the three main components of energy expenditure.::Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR), the thermic effect of food, and physical activity.||What happens to body weight when a person is in positive energy balance for a long period?::They gain weight, because energy intake exceeds energy expenditure.

learning_activity_name: Extract nutrients from selected foods (cereals, milk, coconut, seeds and nuts)
sla_name: Extracting nutrients from selected foods
sla_assessment_criteria: Various nutrients from selected foods are extracted.
sla_teaching_aids: Food items such as cereals|Milk|Coconut|Seeds|Nuts|Laboratory apparatus|Reagents
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Laboratory extraction techniques allow specific nutrients to be separated from a food so that their presence and properties can be studied directly.
sla_notes_details: Extracting nutrients from foods such as cereals, milk, coconut, seeds and nuts uses methods matched to the nutrient being isolated: fat can be extracted from seeds and nuts by pressing or solvent extraction; starch can be extracted from cereals by soaking, grinding and settling; and protein can be separated from milk by techniques such as acid precipitation of casein. Each extraction procedure requires appropriate laboratory apparatus and careful, step-by-step technique to avoid contaminating or destroying the nutrient being studied, and the extracted nutrient is then examined or tested to confirm its identity.
sla_notes_illustrations: To extract oil from coconut in the laboratory, a student would grate and press the coconut flesh, then separate the released oil from the remaining solid material, demonstrating fat extraction using simple mechanical pressing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local oil presses that extract cooking oil from sunflower or coconut, and home methods of separating cream from milk, are everyday, larger-scale applications of the same nutrient extraction principles studied in the laboratory.
sla_exercise: Name one method used to extract fat from seeds or nuts.::Pressing (or solvent extraction).||How can protein be separated from milk in a simple laboratory procedure?::By acid precipitation of casein, causing the protein to separate out.||Why must extraction procedures be carried out carefully and step by step?::To avoid contaminating or destroying the nutrient being studied, ensuring an accurate result.

learning_activity_name: Carry out microscopic observations to examine the structures of different foods
sla_name: Microscopic observation of food structures
sla_assessment_criteria: Microscopic observations to examine the structures of different foods stuff is well conducted.
sla_teaching_aids: Food items laboratory apparatus|Chemicals
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Examining food under a microscope reveals structural details of nutrients and tissues that are invisible to the naked eye, helping to identify and understand food composition.
sla_notes_details: Carrying out microscopic observations of foods involves preparing a thin sample or slide of the food (such as a starch suspension, plant tissue or animal fat sample), placing it under a light microscope at appropriate magnification, and recording and sketching the observed structures such as starch granules (which have characteristic shapes and sizes depending on the plant source), plant cell walls, or fat globules in a sample like milk. Comparing structures under the microscope with reference diagrams helps identify the food source and understand how its structure relates to its nutritional and cooking properties.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student examining a drop of maize starch suspension under a microscope would observe and sketch characteristic polygonal starch granules, then compare their shape and size with potato starch granules, which appear larger and more oval.
sla_notes_daily_life: Food quality laboratories and research institutions use microscopic examination in exactly this way to verify the authenticity and quality of food ingredients sold commercially.
sla_exercise: What is the purpose of examining food under a microscope?::To reveal structural details of nutrients and tissues that are invisible to the naked eye, helping identify and understand food composition.||Give one example of a food structure that can be observed under a microscope.::Starch granules (or plant cell walls, or fat globules).||Why is it useful to compare observed starch granules with reference diagrams?::It helps identify the plant source of the starch and understand its properties.

sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Chemical tests in the laboratory confirm the presence of specific nutrients such as protein, starch and fats in a food sample, and also reveal issues such as rancidity.
sla_notes_details: Common laboratory tests include the biuret test for protein (a violet colour indicates a positive result), the iodine test for starch (a blue-black colour indicates a positive result), and the emulsion test or grease-spot test for fats (a translucent spot on paper indicates the presence of fat). Food rancidity, the development of unpleasant odour and taste in fats due to oxidation or microbial action, can be detected by smell, taste or specific chemical tests. Food toxicants are naturally occurring or contaminant substances that are harmful if consumed in excess, while functional foods are foods that provide health benefits beyond basic nutrition, such as probiotic yogurt.
sla_notes_illustrations: Testing a sample of milk with the biuret reagent and observing a violet colour confirms the presence of protein, while testing a sample of maize porridge with iodine solution and observing a blue-black colour confirms the presence of starch.
sla_notes_daily_life: Food safety inspectors and quality control staff in Tanzanian food processing companies use these same simple laboratory tests to confirm nutrient content and detect problems such as rancidity in food products.
sla_exercise: Which reagent is used to test for protein, and what colour indicates a positive result?::Biuret reagent; a violet colour indicates protein is present.||Which test is used to confirm the presence of starch, and what result is positive?::The iodine test; a blue-black colour is a positive result.||What is food rancidity?::The development of unpleasant odour and taste in fats due to oxidation or microbial action.

specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the determinants of good nutrition and intra-household food distribution
learning_activity_name: Describe determinants of good nutrition (biological, economic, physical and social) and intra-household food distribution
sla_name: Determinants of good nutrition and intra-household food distribution
sla_assessment_criteria: Determinants of good nutrition and intra-household food distribution are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: A chart showing determinants of good nutrition
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Good nutrition depends on more than food availability alone; it is shaped by a combination of biological, economic, physical and social factors, including how food is shared within a household.
sla_notes_details: Biological determinants include age, health status and disease, which affect nutrient needs and absorption. Economic determinants include household income and food prices, which affect what food can be afforded. Physical determinants include access to farmland, water, markets and food storage facilities. Social determinants include cultural food taboos, education level, and gender roles. Intra-household food distribution refers to how available food is shared among household members, which is not always equal; in some households, men or working members may receive larger or better-quality portions than children, women or the elderly, which can cause malnutrition even in food-secure households.
sla_notes_illustrations: A household with enough food overall may still have a malnourished child if cultural practice gives the best portions of meat or fish to the father first, showing how intra-household food distribution, a social determinant, can cause poor nutrition despite adequate food availability.
sla_notes_daily_life: Community nutrition education in Tanzania often addresses these same determinants, encouraging fair distribution of nutritious food among all household members, especially young children and pregnant women.
sla_exercise: Name the four categories of determinants of good nutrition.::Biological, economic, physical and social determinants.||What is meant by intra-household food distribution?::How available food is shared among the members of a household.||Give one reason a household with enough food might still have malnourished members.::Unequal intra-household food distribution, where some members (e.g. children or women) receive smaller or lower-quality portions.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the principles and practices of nutritional assessment
specific_competence_name: Conduct nutritional assessment
learning_activity_name: Describe the methodology used in nutritional assessment (study design, ethics, data collection, analysis and report writing)
sla_name: Methodology used in nutritional assessment
sla_assessment_criteria: Nutritional assessment methods are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Dietary assessment tools
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Nutritional assessment uses a structured research methodology to measure and understand the nutritional status of individuals or communities.
sla_notes_details: The methodology used in nutritional assessment includes selecting an appropriate study design (such as a cross-sectional survey), following research ethics (informed consent, confidentiality and doing no harm to participants), data collection methods (anthropometric measurements such as height and weight, dietary intake recalls, clinical examination for signs of deficiency, and biochemical tests), data analysis (comparing collected data against reference standards to classify nutritional status), and report writing (presenting findings clearly with recommendations for action).
sla_notes_illustrations: A student conducting a simple nutritional assessment of a nearby community would first design a short survey, ensure participants consent and their data stays confidential, then measure children's height and weight, compare the results with growth standards, and write a report identifying any signs of malnutrition found.
sla_notes_daily_life: Government nutrition surveys conducted across Tanzania to monitor child stunting and wasting use exactly this methodology on a much larger scale.
sla_exercise: Name one research ethic that must be followed during nutritional assessment.::Obtaining informed consent from participants (or maintaining confidentiality, or doing no harm).||List three data collection methods used in nutritional assessment.::Anthropometric measurements, dietary intake recall, and clinical examination (or biochemical tests).||What is the purpose of the data analysis stage in nutritional assessment?::To compare collected data against reference standards and classify the nutritional status of individuals or the community.

sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: This competence applies nutritional assessment methodology practically, by conducting a real assessment within a chosen community.
sla_notes_details: Carrying out a nutritional assessment in a selected community involves obtaining permission and community cooperation, selecting a representative sample of individuals or households, applying the planned data collection methods (measuring weight and height, taking dietary recalls, observing clinical signs of malnutrition such as thin hair or swollen limbs), recording data accurately and consistently, and identifying the nutritional problems present, such as stunting, wasting, underweight or micronutrient deficiency, in the assessed population. Findings are then written into a clear report highlighting the main nutritional problems found and the possible next steps.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group of students assessing a nearby village might measure the height and weight of 30 children, calculate how many fall below the expected growth standards, and report that a certain number show signs of stunting due to chronic undernutrition.
sla_notes_daily_life: District and regional nutrition officers in Tanzania carry out this same kind of community nutritional assessment regularly to identify where nutrition interventions are most urgently needed.
sla_exercise: What must be obtained before carrying out a nutritional assessment in a community?::Permission and cooperation from the community.||Name one anthropometric measurement commonly taken during a community nutritional assessment.::Height (or weight).||Give one nutritional problem that a community assessment might identify.::Stunting (or wasting, underweight, or a micronutrient deficiency).

sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The Form V project introduces students to independent, practical investigation of a food or nutrition problem, to be completed and submitted for assessment in Form VI.
sla_notes_details: Designing a project in Food and Nutrition involves choosing a relevant, manageable topic (such as investigating the nutritional value of a local food, assessing feeding practices in a community, or testing a food preservation method), stating clear objectives, planning the methodology (what data or samples will be collected and how), and preparing the necessary tools, such as questionnaires, measuring equipment or laboratory apparatus. The project is then carried out step by step, following the plan, with records kept of all data, observations and any problems encountered so the work can be completed and reported accurately in the following year.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student subject club might design a project to investigate the nutrient content of a locally grown vegetable, planning to collect samples, test them for key nutrients in the laboratory, and record results across several weeks.
sla_notes_daily_life: Health researchers and food scientists in Tanzania design and carry out similar structured investigations when studying local foods or community nutrition problems.
sla_exercise: What should a Food and Nutrition project topic be?::Relevant and manageable, focused on a specific food or nutrition problem.||Name one item that should be included when planning a project.::Clear objectives (or a methodology, or the tools/equipment needed).||Why is it important to keep accurate records while carrying out the project?::So the work can be completed and reported accurately when it is finished and submitted for assessment.

sla_name: Nutritional intervention programmes
sla_method: Think pair share and Group discussion
sla_assessment_criteria: Nutritional intervention programmes are correctly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Fortified foods|Food supplements
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Nutritional intervention programmes are organised efforts to prevent or correct nutrient deficiencies and improve the nutritional status of populations.
sla_notes_details: Common nutritional intervention programmes include Vitamin A supplementation (giving high-dose vitamin A capsules to young children to prevent blindness and boost immunity), iron and folic acid supplementation (given to pregnant women to prevent anaemia and neural tube defects), food fortification (adding micronutrients such as iodine to salt or vitamin A to cooking oil during processing), exclusive breastfeeding promotion (encouraging mothers to feed infants only breast milk for the first six months), nutritional education (teaching communities about balanced diets and good feeding practices), deworming (treating intestinal worms that reduce nutrient absorption, especially in children), and HIV and AIDS nutrition interventions (providing nutritional support to people living with HIV to maintain their health and strengthen immunity). Each programme targets a specific nutritional risk and is usually implemented through health facilities, schools or community outreach.
sla_notes_illustrations: A national programme distributing vitamin A capsules to children under five during immunisation campaigns is a direct example of a nutritional intervention programme aimed at preventing vitamin A deficiency.
sla_notes_daily_life: Health centres across Tanzania run several of these programmes routinely, such as giving iron and folic acid tablets to pregnant women during antenatal visits and salt iodisation to prevent goitre.
sla_exercise: Name three nutritional intervention programmes.::Vitamin A supplementation, iron and folic acid supplementation, and food fortification (any three valid examples).||What is the purpose of iron and folic acid supplementation for pregnant women?::To prevent anaemia in the mother and neural tube defects in the developing baby.||Give one example of food fortification.::Adding iodine to salt (or vitamin A to cooking oil).

learning_activity_name: Carry out laboratory analysis to determine minerals in foods
sla_name: Laboratory analysis to determine minerals in food
sla_assessment_criteria: Laboratory analysis to determine minerals in food is well conducted.
sla_teaching_aids: Food items|Laboratory apparatus|Chemical reagents
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Determining the mineral content of food in the laboratory allows the actual amount of minerals such as iron, calcium or zinc present in a food sample to be measured.
sla_notes_details: Laboratory analysis to determine minerals in food typically involves ashing the food sample (burning off organic material at high temperature to leave behind mineral ash), dissolving the ash in an appropriate acid, and using a chemical or instrumental method, such as titration or a colorimetric test, to measure the concentration of a specific mineral in the resulting solution. Results are then compared with expected values or standards to assess whether a food is a good source of that mineral. Accurate technique, correct use of laboratory apparatus and careful handling of chemical reagents are essential to obtain reliable results.
sla_notes_illustrations: To determine iron content in a food sample, a student would first ash the sample to remove organic matter, dissolve the resulting ash in acid, and then use a colour-based chemical test to estimate the amount of iron present based on the intensity of colour produced.
sla_notes_daily_life: Food quality laboratories that certify the mineral content claimed on packaged food labels in Tanzania use this same ashing and chemical analysis procedure.
sla_exercise: What is the first step in determining mineral content in a food sample?::Ashing the sample, burning off organic material at high temperature to leave behind mineral ash.||Why is the ash dissolved in acid during mineral analysis?::To bring the minerals into solution so their concentration can be measured chemically.||Why must laboratory apparatus and chemical reagents be handled carefully during this analysis?::To ensure accurate, reliable results and to prevent accidents or contamination.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the technology for processing and preserving food
specific_competence_name: Process and preserve different types of food
learning_activity_name: Apply modern methods to process food (milling, canning and bottling, fermentation, pasteurization, sterilization, dehydration, pickling)
sla_name: Modern methods of food processing
sla_assessment_criteria: Different food stuffs are well processed using modern methods.
sla_teaching_aids: Processed foods such as fermented|Pasteurized milk|Laboratory apparatus|Chemical reagents|Heat sources|Food items
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Food processing methods transform raw food into safer, more convenient or longer-lasting forms using techniques ranging from simple heat treatment to chemical preservation.
sla_notes_details: Modern methods of processing food include milling (grinding grains into flour), canning and bottling (sealing food in containers and heat-treating it to destroy micro-organisms for long shelf life), fermentation (using micro-organisms to convert food components, as in yoghurt or fermented porridge), pasteurization (heating liquids such as milk to a temperature that destroys harmful micro-organisms without fully cooking the product), sterilization (heating food to a higher temperature than pasteurization to destroy all micro-organisms and their spores), dehydration (removing water to prevent microbial growth, as in dried fish or dried fruit), and pickling (preserving food in an acidic or salty solution). Each method is chosen based on the food type, the desired shelf life, and the resources available.
sla_notes_illustrations: Milk sold in Tanzanian shops is usually pasteurized, heated briefly to destroy harmful bacteria while keeping most of its nutrients and fresh taste, unlike sterilized milk which is treated at a higher temperature for a much longer shelf life.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local food processors making fermented porridge (togwa), sun-dried fish, and canned fruit juices are all applying these same modern food processing methods on a small or large scale in Tanzania.
sla_exercise: Name three modern methods of processing food.::Milling, canning/bottling, and pasteurization (any three valid methods).||What is the difference between pasteurization and sterilization?::Pasteurization heats food to a lower temperature that destroys harmful micro-organisms while sterilization uses a higher temperature to destroy all micro-organisms and their spores.||Give one example of a fermented food.::Yoghurt (or fermented porridge/togwa).

learning_activity_name: Conduct laboratory analysis to determine the effect of heat and air on selected foods
sla_name: Effects of heat and air on selected foods
sla_assessment_criteria: Laboratory analysis to determine the effect of heat and air on selected foods is well conducted.
sla_teaching_aids: Food items|Kitchen equipment|Laboratory apparatus|Chemical reagents|Heat sources
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Heat and air (oxygen) can both cause significant, sometimes undesirable, changes in food during cooking, processing and storage.
sla_notes_details: Heat causes physical and chemical changes such as protein denaturation (proteins changing structure and texture, as seen when an egg cooks), starch gelatinization (starch granules swelling and thickening a liquid, as in porridge), loss of heat-sensitive vitamins such as vitamin C, and browning reactions that develop colour and flavour. Air, specifically oxygen, causes oxidation, which leads to rancidity in fats and oils (unpleasant odour and taste) and browning of cut fruits and vegetables (enzymatic browning) when their cells are exposed to oxygen. Laboratory analysis of these effects involves exposing food samples to controlled heat or air conditions and observing changes in colour, texture, smell and nutrient content.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student conducting a laboratory experiment might cut an apple in half, leave one half exposed to air and cover the other, then observe that the exposed half browns due to oxidation while the covered half stays fresh longer.
sla_notes_daily_life: Cooking vegetables briefly rather than for a long time to preserve vitamin C, and storing cut fruit in an airtight container to prevent browning, are everyday applications of understanding the effects of heat and air on food.
sla_exercise: What happens to proteins when they are exposed to heat, using egg white as an example?::They denature, changing structure and texture from a liquid to a solid form.||What causes enzymatic browning in a cut fruit or vegetable?::Exposure of the cut surface to oxygen in the air, which triggers a browning reaction.||Name one vitamin that is easily destroyed by heat during cooking.::Vitamin C.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the technology for processing and preserving food
specific_competence_name: Process and preserve different types of food
learning_activity_name: Carry out laboratory analysis to determine the actions of raising agents
sla_name: Actions of raising agents in food
sla_assessment_criteria: Laboratory analysis to determine the actions of raising agents is well conducted.
sla_teaching_aids: Laboratory apparatus|Chemical reagents|Raising agents|Heat sources|Food items
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Raising agents are substances used in cooking and baking to make dough or batter rise by producing gas, giving baked products a light, airy texture.
sla_notes_details: Common raising agents include baking powder and baking soda (bicarbonate of soda), which release carbon dioxide gas when they react with moisture and, in some cases, an acid ingredient or heat; yeast, a living micro-organism that produces carbon dioxide through fermentation of sugars, also producing flavour compounds; and steam or air, which are physical raising agents that expand when heated, as in choux pastry or whisked egg foams. Laboratory analysis of raising agents involves testing how much gas or volume increase each agent produces under controlled conditions, and observing the texture of the final baked product.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student comparing bread made with yeast to a scone made with baking powder would observe that the yeasted bread takes longer to rise (through fermentation) but develops a distinct flavour, while the scone rises quickly through the chemical reaction of baking powder.
sla_notes_daily_life: Bakers making bread, mandazi and cakes across Tanzania rely daily on understanding how different raising agents behave to produce the texture they want in their products.
sla_exercise: Name two chemical raising agents used in baking.::Baking powder and baking soda (bicarbonate of soda).||How does yeast act as a raising agent?::It ferments sugars in the dough, producing carbon dioxide gas that makes the dough rise.||Give one example of a physical raising agent.::Steam (or air, as in whisked egg foam).

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the technology for processing and preserving food
specific_competence_name: Process and preserve different types of food
learning_activity_name: Describe the biochemistry of food preservation (principles and modern methods of food preservation)
sla_name: Biochemistry of food preservation
sla_method: ICT based learning and Group discussion
sla_assessment_criteria: The biochemistry of food preservation is clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures/ videos showing modern methods of food preservation
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Understanding the biochemistry behind food preservation explains why different preservation methods successfully prevent food spoilage.
sla_notes_details: Food preservation methods work through several biochemical principles: reducing water activity (removing or binding water so micro-organisms cannot grow, as in dehydration, salting or sugaring), controlling temperature (cold slows microbial growth and enzyme activity, while heat destroys micro-organisms and inactivates enzymes), controlling pH (acidic conditions, as in pickling, inhibit the growth of most spoilage bacteria), and excluding oxygen (vacuum packing or canning prevents oxidation and the growth of aerobic micro-organisms). Modern methods of food preservation apply one or more of these principles, often combined, to extend shelf life while retaining as much nutritional and sensory quality as possible.
sla_notes_illustrations: Salting fish before drying it works because the added salt draws out water and lowers water activity in the fish tissue, creating an environment where spoilage micro-organisms cannot survive, illustrating the water-activity principle of preservation.
sla_notes_daily_life: Refrigerating leftover food at home, drying fish in coastal Tanzanian communities, and pickling vegetables in vinegar are everyday applications of these same biochemical preservation principles.
sla_exercise: Name one biochemical principle used in food preservation.::Reducing water activity (or controlling temperature, controlling pH, or excluding oxygen).||Why does refrigeration help preserve food?::Cold temperatures slow down microbial growth and enzyme activity that cause spoilage.||How does pickling in an acidic solution preserve food?::The acidic conditions inhibit the growth of most spoilage bacteria.

sla_name: Modern methods of preserving food
sla_assessment_criteria: Modern methods preserving food are correctly applied.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures/ videos showing modern methods of food preservation|Chemical preservatives|Heat sources|Preservation equipment|Food items
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Applying modern preservation methods practically extends the shelf life of food using techniques such as chemical addition, freezing, canning and bottling.
sla_notes_details: Applying modern methods to preserve food includes adding permitted chemical preservatives (such as sodium benzoate or sulphur dioxide) at safe, regulated concentrations to inhibit microbial growth, freezing food at very low temperatures to stop microbial activity and slow enzyme action while keeping the food largely intact, and canning and bottling, which combines heat treatment with an airtight seal to destroy micro-organisms and prevent recontamination. Selecting the appropriate method depends on the food type, the desired shelf life, available equipment, and cost, since freezing requires reliable electricity while canning and chemical preservation do not.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student subject club preserving tomatoes might can them in sealed, heat-treated jars, allowing the tomatoes to remain usable for many months without refrigeration, since the combination of heat and an airtight seal destroys and excludes spoilage micro-organisms.
sla_notes_daily_life: Households freezing meat and fish, and food companies canning fruits, vegetables and fish for sale in Tanzanian markets, are practical everyday applications of these modern preservation methods.
sla_exercise: Name two modern methods of preserving food.::Freezing and canning/bottling (or adding chemical preservatives).||Give one example of a chemical preservative used in food.::Sodium benzoate (or sulphur dioxide).||Why might a household choose canning over freezing to preserve food?::Canning does not require reliable electricity or a freezer, unlike freezing.

specific_competence_name: Process and preserve different types of food
learning_activity_name: Conduct laboratory analysis to determine the effects of preservation on selected foods
sla_name: Effects of preservation on selected foods
sla_assessment_criteria: Laboratory analysis to determine the effect of preservation on selected foods is well conducted.
sla_teaching_aids: Kitchen equipment|Food preservatives|Heat sources|Food items
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: While preservation methods extend shelf life, they can also cause changes in the nutritional value, texture, flavour and appearance of the food being preserved.
sla_notes_details: Effects of preservation on food include some loss of heat-sensitive vitamins (such as vitamin C) during canning or pasteurization, changes in texture (freezing can cause ice crystals that damage cell structure, making thawed fruits and vegetables softer), changes in flavour and colour (drying concentrates flavour but can darken colour, while chemical preservatives may leave a slight taste), and, when done correctly, a significant reduction in microbial spoilage that keeps the food safe to eat for a longer period. Laboratory analysis of these effects involves comparing a preserved food sample with a fresh sample for nutrient content, texture, colour and microbial safety.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student comparing fresh spinach with canned spinach in the laboratory might find that the canned spinach has lower vitamin C content and a softer texture, illustrating the typical effects of heat-based preservation.
sla_notes_daily_life: Consumers choosing between fresh and preserved foods in the market, such as fresh versus dried fish, are making decisions based on exactly these trade-offs between shelf life and nutritional or sensory quality.
sla_exercise: Name one nutrient commonly lost during heat-based food preservation.::Vitamin C.||How does freezing affect the texture of fruits and vegetables after thawing?::Ice crystals formed during freezing can damage cell structure, making the thawed food softer.||What is the main benefit of preservation despite these changes?::A significant reduction in microbial spoilage, keeping the food safe to eat for longer.

specific_competence_name: Process and preserve different types of food
learning_activity_name: Conduct laboratory analysis to identify effect of acids and alkali on food
sla_name: Effect of acids and alkali on food
sla_assessment_criteria: Laboratory analysis to identify the effect of acids and alkali on foods is well conducted.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures/ videos showing effects of acids or alkalis on food|Laboratory apparatus|Chemical reagents|Heat sources|Food items
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Acids and alkalis change the chemical structure, texture, colour and safety of food in ways that are important both for cooking and for preservation.
sla_notes_details: Acids (such as vinegar, lemon juice or lactic acid from fermentation) can denature proteins (as in ceviche-style 'cooking' of fish with lime juice), change the colour of some plant pigments, inhibit the growth of many spoilage bacteria (making them useful in pickling), and soften some plant fibres. Alkalis (such as baking soda) can soften plant cell walls and speed cooking of some vegetables and legumes, but excessive alkalinity can destroy heat-sensitive vitamins such as vitamin C and vitamin B1, and can alter colour and flavour undesirably. Laboratory analysis of these effects involves treating food samples with acidic or alkaline solutions and comparing texture, colour and nutrient retention with an untreated control sample.
sla_notes_illustrations: Adding a small amount of baking soda (an alkali) to cooking beans can soften them faster, but a student testing this in the laboratory would find that it also reduces the vitamin C content compared with beans cooked without baking soda.
sla_notes_daily_life: Marinating meat in lemon juice or vinegar before cooking, a common household practice in Tanzania, is a direct everyday application of how acids affect the texture and flavour of food.
sla_exercise: Name one everyday acid used in food preparation.::Vinegar (or lemon juice).||How can an alkali such as baking soda affect the nutrient content of cooked vegetables?::It can destroy heat-sensitive vitamins such as vitamin C and vitamin B1.||Why are acids sometimes added when pickling food?::Because the acidic conditions inhibit the growth of many spoilage bacteria, helping preserve the food.

specific_competence_name: Process and preserve different types of food
learning_activity_name: Carry out laboratory analysis to determine spoilage microorganisms in food
sla_name: Determining spoilage microorganisms in food
sla_assessment_criteria: Microorganisms affecting food are clearly described. Laboratory analysis to determine spoilage microorganisms in food is well conducted.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures/ videos showing microbial spoilage foods|Laboratory apparatus|Chemical reagent|Microscope|Heat sources|Food items
sla_references: TET(2023), FOOD AND HUMAN NUTRITION SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Identifying the micro-organisms responsible for spoiling food helps explain why food goes bad and how spoilage can be prevented or controlled.
sla_notes_details: Determining spoilage microorganisms in food involves preparing a sample of spoiled or suspect food, culturing it under conditions that encourage microbial growth (such as an agar plate incubated at a suitable temperature), and observing the growth for characteristics such as colony shape, colour and smell, or examining samples under a microscope to identify bacteria, yeasts or moulds present. Common spoilage micro-organisms include bacteria that cause souring or off odours, yeasts that cause fermentation and gas production in stored juices, and moulds that grow visibly on bread, fruit and grains, sometimes producing harmful toxins.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student examining mouldy bread under a microscope after culturing a sample would observe thread-like fungal structures (hyphae) confirming that mould, rather than bacteria, is responsible for the visible spoilage.
sla_notes_daily_life: Recognising the visible mould on stale bread or the sour smell of spoiled milk at home is an everyday, informal version of identifying spoilage micro-organisms studied formally in this competence.
sla_exercise: What is the purpose of culturing a food sample on an agar plate?::To encourage microbial growth so the type of spoilage micro-organism present can be identified.||Name one type of micro-organism responsible for food spoilage.::Bacteria (or yeasts, or moulds).||Why is it important to identify the spoilage micro-organisms present in food?::It helps explain why the food spoiled and guides appropriate methods to prevent or control future spoilage.

sla_notes_intro: The Form VI stage of the project requires students to finalise, complete and formally submit for assessment the investigation they designed and began in Form V.
sla_notes_details: Completing and submitting the project involves reviewing the objectives and plan set out in Form V, finishing any remaining data collection, sample analysis or fieldwork, organising and analysing all collected data to draw clear conclusions, writing a complete project report that includes an introduction, methodology, results, discussion and conclusion, and formatting the report according to the required assessment guidelines before submitting it. Group discussion and peer review before submission help identify gaps or errors that should be corrected while there is still time.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student club that began investigating the nutrient content of a local vegetable in Form V would, in Form VI, finish the remaining laboratory tests, compile all results into tables, write a full discussion comparing their findings with expected values, and submit the completed report for assessment.
sla_notes_daily_life: Completing and submitting a structured piece of work on schedule, as required here, is the same discipline needed later for professional reports in health, food science or any research-based career.
sla_exercise: What must be reviewed at the start of completing the Form VI project?::The objectives and plan set out for the project in Form V.||Name three sections that should be included in the final project report.::Introduction, methodology and results (or discussion and conclusion).||Why is peer review useful before submitting the final project report?::It helps identify gaps or errors that can still be corrected before the report is submitted for assessment.
